before.question: Which assessment is most appropriate for arthropod transmission?
choices: Assess tick or fly exposure, location, season, animal contact, skin portal, and symptom onset
Assess travel, animal death, eschar, mediastinal findings, blood counts, cultures, imaging, and exposure cluster
Assess time to treatment, swallowing, cations, tube feeds, esophageal risk, photosensitivity, pregnancy context, and response
Assess imaging, source control, cultures, echocardiography, joint or bone findings, organ function, and response
before.rationale: Tularemia has a distinct vector ecology from Lyme disease

after.question: When assessing possible arthropod-associated tularemia, which exposure assessment is most appropriate?
choices: Assess tick or fly exposure, location, season, animal contact, skin portal, and symptom onset
Assume the Lyme disease tick pathway is a complete tularemia exposure assessment.
Exclude tularemia whenever a patient cannot recall a tick bite, without asking about deer flies or animal contact.
Use the bite location alone and disregard exposure timing or the clinical presentation.
after.rationale: Tick or deer-fly exposure can be relevant, and animal contact is another route. Tularemia vector ecology differs from Lyme disease; an exposure history should not be reduced to Lyme-specific assumptions or a remembered tick bite.

perQuestionReview.sourceBasis: CDC clinical signs and MMWR introduction

before.question: Which assessment is most appropriate for incubation and transmission?
choices: Assess exposure date, symptom onset, laboratory or occupational contact, PPE breach, and intentional release indicators
Assess who received the alert, specimen route, containment, potential aerosol generation, and occupational exposure
Assess antacids, iron, calcium, magnesium, tube feeds, QT drugs, tendon disease, neuropathy, glycemia, and aortic history
Assess exact weight, age, renal function, concentration, maximum dose, caregiver technique, and response
before.rationale: Ordinary close contact is not the exposure pattern that drives tularemia spread

after.question: When reconstructing a suspected tularemia exposure, which timeline and contact assessment is most appropriate?
choices: Assess exposure date, symptom onset, laboratory or occupational contact, PPE breach, and intentional release indicators
Use symptom onset alone to identify the exposure route, without asking when or how contact occurred.
Assume routine proximity to a patient carries the same risk as direct contact with infectious material.
Disregard laboratory or occupational safety breaches because the illness can also follow natural exposures.
after.rationale: Relate symptom onset to the exposure date and mechanism. Occupational or infectious-material contact requires its own assessment; ordinary close contact is not the usual transmission route. Rare human-associated transmissions have been reported, so an absolute claim that transmission has never occurred is inappropriate.

perQuestionReview.sourceBasis: CDC clinical signs; MMWR introduction and PPE

before.question: Which assessment is most appropriate for ulceroglandular disease?
choices: Assess ulcer, eschar, pain, drainage, node size, fluctuation, fever, and exposure portal
Assess portal, lesion age, prior therapy, collection technique, transport, culture, PCR, and tissue needs
Assess swallowing, esophageal disease, supplements, antacids, tube feeds, photosensitivity, nausea, and adherence
Assess maternal timing and treatment, neonatal symptoms, cultures, CSF, renal function, drug levels, and organ support
before.rationale: The skin portal and regional node pattern reveal the inoculation route

after.question: When evaluating possible ulceroglandular tularemia, which local examination and exposure assessment is most appropriate?
choices: Assess ulcer, eschar, pain, drainage, node size, fluctuation, fever, and exposure portal
Treat the skin lesion alone as definitive confirmation without considering exposure or diagnostic evidence.
Exclude glandular tularemia whenever no obvious skin ulcer is found.
Assess only respiratory findings and ignore the lesion and its regional lymph nodes.
after.rationale: Ulceroglandular disease can produce an inoculation-site ulcer with regional lymphadenopathy after an arthropod bite or animal contact. Glandular disease may lack an obvious ulcer. The pattern supports assessment but does not independently prove the cause.

perQuestionReview.sourceBasis: CDC clinical signs and MMWR introduction

before.question: Which assessment is most appropriate for dangerous mimics?
choices: Assess travel, animal death, eschar, mediastinal findings, blood counts, cultures, imaging, and exposure cluster
Assess time to treatment, swallowing, cations, tube feeds, esophageal risk, photosensitivity, pregnancy context, and response
Assess imaging, source control, cultures, echocardiography, joint or bone findings, organ function, and response
Assess fever, nodes, respiratory status, organ function, adverse effects, adherence, pending results, and contact route
before.rationale: Several mimics require different isolation, prophylaxis, or immediate treatment

after.question: When a positive tularemia antibody result does not fit the patient's illness and exposure history, which assessment is most appropriate before accepting the diagnosis?
choices: Reassess the clinical syndrome, exposure history, test timing and specificity, and alternative causes of illness.
Treat any positive antibody result as proof of the cause of the current illness, regardless of clinical or exposure fit.
Stop evaluating other causes as soon as an antibody result is positive.
Use the antibody result alone to identify the exposure portal and current illness severity.
after.rationale: Interpret antibody results with a compatible clinical illness and exposure. False positives and cross-reactions can occur, and antibodies can persist after prior infection. An isolated result does not establish that tularemia explains the current illness; poor clinical fit warrants reassessment of alternatives.

perQuestionReview.sourceBasis: CDC testing: serologic interpretation, persistence, false positives and cross-reactions

before.question: Which assessment is most appropriate for laboratory alert?
choices: Assess who received the alert, specimen route, containment, potential aerosol generation, and occupational exposure
Assess antacids, iron, calcium, magnesium, tube feeds, QT drugs, tendon disease, neuropathy, glycemia, and aortic history
Assess exact weight, age, renal function, concentration, maximum dose, caregiver technique, and response
Assess dose and duration, route, cations, renal adjustment, vomiting, node abscess, meningitis, alternative pathogens, and susceptibility context
before.rationale: F. tularensis creates a serious laboratory acquired infection hazard

after.question: When tularemia is suspected before a clinical specimen is processed, which laboratory-safety assessment is most appropriate?
choices: Assess who received the alert, specimen route, containment, potential aerosol generation, and occupational exposure
Use routine processing without alerting the laboratory because the specimen is clinical material.
Wait for a positive culture before notifying laboratory staff of the suspected organism.
Treat patient-care precautions as proof that all laboratory culture work can proceed without organism-specific safety review.
after.rationale: Notify the laboratory when tularemia is suspected so staff can plan appropriate diagnostic and safety procedures. Clinical-specimen and culture handling are distinct; an alert should precede hazardous work rather than depend on a positive culture.

perQuestionReview.sourceBasis: CDC testing; CDC reducing risk; MMWR laboratory PPE

before.question: Which assessment is most appropriate for specimen selection?
choices: Assess portal, lesion age, prior therapy, collection technique, transport, culture, PCR, and tissue needs
Assess swallowing, esophageal disease, supplements, antacids, tube feeds, photosensitivity, nausea, and adherence
Assess maternal timing and treatment, neonatal symptoms, cultures, CSF, renal function, drug levels, and organ support
Assess understanding, teach back, dosing schedule, cations, hydration, sun, tendon or neurologic symptoms, hearing, fever, and access
before.rationale: Diagnostic yield depends on matching the specimen to the disease compartment

after.question: Which assessment best supports selecting diagnostic specimens when tularemia is suspected?
choices: Match the specimen to the clinical form and coordinate safe collection and testing with the alerted laboratory.
Choose the same specimen for every clinical form without considering the involved site.
Use an early negative antibody test to cancel all further diagnostic assessment despite compatible illness.
Collect and process specimens without informing the laboratory of suspected tularemia.
after.rationale: Specimen choice follows the disease compartment: ulcer, conjunctival, lymph-node, blood or respiratory material may be appropriate. Alert the laboratory and coordinate testing. An early negative antibody result does not exclude compatible acute disease.

perQuestionReview.sourceBasis: CDC testing: specimens and serologic window

before.question: Which assessment is most appropriate for occupational exposure PEP?
choices: Assess exposure type, aerosol or sharps event, PPE, timing, symptoms, contraindications, adherence, and public health guidance
Assess tick or fly exposure, location, season, animal contact, skin portal, and symptom onset
Assess travel, animal death, eschar, mediastinal findings, blood counts, cultures, imaging, and exposure cluster
Assess time to treatment, swallowing, cations, tube feeds, esophageal risk, photosensitivity, pregnancy context, and response
before.rationale: PEP uses lower or shorter exposures because clinical disease is not yet established

after.question: For an asymptomatic worker with a possible occupational exposure to F. tularensis, which assessment is most appropriate before choosing prophylaxis or fever watch?
choices: Assess the material and exposure mechanism, safety breaches, elapsed time, symptoms, and individual risk to choose prophylaxis or fever watch with clinical and occupational-health guidance.
Give the same prophylaxis plan to every worker based only on being employed in the same laboratory.
Choose prophylaxis or monitoring without reviewing the exposure mechanism or elapsed time.
Continue an exposure-prevention plan unchanged after concerning symptoms develop, without clinical evaluation.
after.rationale: Occupational management may use antimicrobial prophylaxis or fever watch. Exposure risk, elapsed time, and individual preferences help guide the decision; criteria are not fully standardized. New concerning symptoms require medical evaluation for illness. Prophylaxis is not treatment for an already symptomatic patient.

perQuestionReview.sourceBasis: CDC occupational exposure updated September16,2026; MMWR occupational section

before.question: Which assessment is most appropriate for intentional release response?
choices: Assess exposure zone, symptom screen, release timing, drug supply, resistance intelligence, contraindications, and follow-up
Assess exposure date, symptom onset, laboratory or occupational contact, PPE breach, and intentional release indicators
Assess who received the alert, specimen route, containment, potential aerosol generation, and occupational exposure
Assess antacids, iron, calcium, magnesium, tube feeds, QT drugs, tendon disease, neuropathy, glycemia, and aortic history
before.rationale: Illness changes the objective from prevention to treatment under resistance uncertainty

after.question: When an intentional F. tularensis release is suspected, which assessment best separates prevention from treatment needs?
choices: Assess exposure zone, symptom screen, release timing, drug supply, resistance intelligence, contraindications, and follow-up
Give one prophylaxis plan to symptomatic and asymptomatic people without reassessing illness.
Assume every nearby resident has confirmed exposure without an event investigation.
Disregard antimicrobial susceptibility information once prophylaxis has started.
after.rationale: Define who was likely exposed and who is already ill, with public-health coordination. Prevention and treatment have different objectives, and possible engineered resistance affects antimicrobial decisions. Exposure location, timing, symptoms, available drugs and follow-up therefore belong in the assessment.

perQuestionReview.sourceBasis: CDC event response August27,2026; MMWR release response

before.question: Which assessment is most appropriate for no routine PrEP?
choices: Assess job role, PPE, specimen handling, aerosol event, sharps injury, symptoms, and public health instructions
Assess ulcer, eschar, pain, drainage, node size, fluctuation, fever, and exposure portal
Assess portal, lesion age, prior therapy, collection technique, transport, culture, PCR, and tissue needs
Assess swallowing, esophageal disease, supplements, antacids, tube feeds, photosensitivity, nausea, and adherence
before.rationale: Unnecessary prophylaxis creates toxicity and resistance without a demonstrated transmission benefit

after.question: For a healthcare worker using standard precautions during routine tularemia care, which prevention assessment is most appropriate?
choices: Assess job role, PPE, specimen handling, aerosol event, sharps injury, symptoms, and public health instructions
Start routine antimicrobial PrEP for every patient-contact shift regardless of exposure.
Replace protective measures with routine pre-exposure antibiotics.
Use the healthcare job title alone to decide prophylaxis without considering actual exposure.
after.rationale: Routine patient care with standard precautions does not require automatic antimicrobial PrEP. Review the actual task and exposure. Contaminated environmental response work without appropriate PPE is a separate situation requiring individualized public-health guidance, rather than a rule that prophylaxis is never considered.

perQuestionReview.sourceBasis: MMWR PrEP/PEP and environmental-response exception; CDC occupational guidance

teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.heading: Place symptoms on the clock
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.before: Symptoms usually begin after several days, although the range is broader. Person to person transmission has not been demonstrated, so routine household contact is not the exposure that drives prophylaxis decisions.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.after: Symptoms typically begin 3 to 5 days after exposure, with a reported range of 1 to 14 days. Ordinary close contact is not the usual transmission route, although rare human-associated transmissions have been reported. Assess the actual contact, including occupational or infectious-material exposure.

teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.heading: Match specimen to form
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.before: Ulcer material, conjunctival swab, node aspirate or biopsy, blood, respiratory material, and pleural fluid can be considered according to anatomy and laboratory guidance. Prior therapy and lesion age affect yield.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.after: Choose ulcer scrapings, conjunctival swabs, lymph-node aspirates or biopsies, blood, or respiratory material, including pleural fluid, according to the clinical form and laboratory guidance. Alert the laboratory when tularemia is suspected; culture may require extended incubation because the organism is fastidious and slow growing.

teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.heading: Use occupational PEP precisely
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.before: Adults can receive ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days, levofloxacin 500 mg orally every 24 hours for 7 days, or doxycycline 100 mg orally every 12 hours for 10 to 14 days after a recognized high risk exposure.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.after: For nonpregnant adults when PEP is chosen, options include ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days, levofloxacin 500 mg orally every 24 hours for 7 days, or doxycycline 100 mg orally every 12 hours for 10 to 14 days. The exposure-risk assessment may instead favor fever watch, particularly for lower-risk exposures. Review elapsed time, safety breaches, and individual preferences with clinical and occupational-health support; new concerning symptoms require evaluation for illness.

teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.heading: Avoid routine pre-exposure antibiotics
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.before: First responders, health care workers using standard precautions, and the general public do not need routine antimicrobial PrEP because person to person transmission risk is low.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.after: Routine antimicrobial PrEP is not recommended for healthcare workers providing patient care or for the general public. Appropriate precautions remain essential. Environmental response crews entering a contaminated release area are a separate situation: if they cannot avoid the area and appropriate EPA-recommended PPE is unavailable, PrEP, PEP, or postexposure fever monitoring may be considered with authorities.

scopedKeyPointCorrections.before: PEP and treatment use different exposure.
scopedKeyPointCorrections.after: Separate exposed people without clinical illness from patients who need treatment evaluation.

sourceDiscrepanciesAndLimits: The whole-book text locator found PDF396/printed388. That table gives organism and an older divided aminoglycoside treatment regimen; it does not support the detailed exposure, diagnosis, or prophylaxis questions. Locator absence is not proof of absence in scanned material.
Approved CDC sources supply the reviewed exposure/diagnosis/prophylaxis claims; occupational guidance is dated September16,2026 and event guidance August27,2026.

CDC reducing-risk summary says no person-to-person transmission; the2025 MMWR documents rare direct-inoculation and transplant-associated transmission and no respiratory transmission. The more specific report controls the repaired absolute claim.
PEP choice is risk-dependent and criteria are not fully standardized. Routine PrEP guidance is not an absolute prohibition covering unprotected contaminated environmental-response work.
Table2 adult PEP doses/durations and relevant notes were actually inspected; unrelated pediatric rows and existing treatment-dose questions are not newly qualified.

Four whole teaching bodies and one scoped key point are revised; other teaching, checks, figures and questions remain unchanged and unqualified by this unit. No whole lesson/module/chapter or full-goal closure.
